newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Moroccan finance minister rules out devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Moroccan finance minister rules out devaluation.

text.p: Morocco's finance minister has ruled out devaluation of the dirham despite pressures from some exporters who want to make their goods more competitive.
"If we devalue, there is the debt and other import factors which would become more expensive," Mohamed Kabbaj was quoted as saying on Wednesday in the newspaper Le Matin du Sahara.
A finance ministry official confirmed that the newspaper report was an accurate summary of an interview carried by a private television network in Casablanca.
Devaluation would also cause difficulties for exporters because raw materials would be more costly, the minister said.

The dirham was not fixed but linked to a basket of currencies and fluctuated accordingly. "It is because of that, that we believe, for the moment, there is no question of devaluing nor of thinking of devaluation," Kabbaj said.
He said one of Morocco's main handicaps was its debt which it had made "enormous efforts" to repay. Foreign debt of $22 billion, and internal debt, consumed 45 percent of the country's resources.
He said Morocco "should not have indebted itself to this level."

The government had an "extremely precise" strategy to deal with the debt problem -- ending the budget deficit, reducing the debt burden by intelligent management, and replacing expensive debt by cheaper debt.
It was also trying to arrange further debt swaps with other countries. France has converted $115 million of debt into funds for investment in Morocco, and Spain has similarly converted $50 million.

Kabbaj said foreign debt, which at the end of the 1980s represented 130 percent of gross domestic product, would be 60 percent at the end of this year, and Morocco hoped to get this down to 40 percent before the year 2000.
Internal debt cost Morocco even more and he wanted to achieve a savings rate of at least 25 to 27 percent against the present 19 percent.

One of Morocco's main challenges was to create 250,000 new jobs each year. The government saw the answer as economic growth and its strategy was based essentially on three factors: increasing exports which should grow 10 to 15 percent a year, increasing investment, and reducing social disparities, particularly between the rural and urban sectors.
